title: What does a strong "Why consulting?" answer sound like, compared with a weak one?
description: Weak and strong example answers to "Why consulting?", with a critique of each, so you can see exactly what interviewers are listening for.
hook: A strong "Why consulting?" answer ties your motivation to a specific moment you enjoyed, shows you understand what consultants actually do, and explains why now; a weak one lists reasons that could describe any career, like smart people and interesting problems. Everyone prepares this question, so interviewers hear the same lines again and again. Seeing weak and strong answers side by side makes the difference obvious.
body:
What the interviewer is listening for

Three things, in roughly 60 seconds:

  1. Evidence. A real moment from your experience when you did consulting-like work and enjoyed it.
  2. Understanding. Proof you know what the job involves: ambiguous problems, analysis, client relationships, long hours and implementation, not just presenting slides. If you are unsure, read what consultants do all day.
  3. Timing. Why this is the right step for you now.

A weak answer

I want to work with smart people, solve interesting problems and learn a lot quickly. Consulting also has great exit opportunities.

Why it falls short: every candidate could say this, and it could describe dozens of careers. It gives no evidence. Mentioning exit opportunities first suggests you are already planning to leave.

A strong answer

This example is illustrative, including the names; use the shape with your own details.

Two things. First, the work itself. In my last role I spent three months working out why one product line was losing money. I interviewed the sales team, rebuilt the cost allocation and found the line was carrying costs from another part of the business. It was the most energised I've been at work, and I want that to be my job, not a side project. Second, the pace of learning. When I spoke to Ana and Jamal at your firm, both said they'd worked in four industries in their first two years. I learn best by being thrown into new problems, and I can't think of another job that gives that breadth this early.

Why it works: it opens with a signpost ("Two things"), gives evidence from real experience, references real conversations, and focuses on the work rather than what comes after. The interviewer can follow up on any part of it.

A second example

At a logistics company, I was asked to find out why one region kept missing deliveries. I built the analysis, interviewed dispatchers and helped redesign how jobs were assigned. What I enjoyed most was going from a vague question to a decision with measurable results. I want to work on that kind of problem more often, across different businesses. I also know the job involves detail, client relationships and implementation, not just presenting, and that's part of the appeal.

This one is credible because the motivation can be traced to behaviour, and the last line shows realism about the job.

"Why this firm?" needs its own reason

Interviewers often ask both together. For the firm, give a separate, checkable reason:

  • a conversation with someone there and what struck you;
  • an industry or practice area the firm is strong in that matches your interests;
  • how the firm staffs projects or develops new joiners, as people there described it;
  • the specific role or office.

Avoid claims about a "unique culture" drawn only from recruitment pages. A useful stress test: delete the firm's name from your answer. Could the same sentence describe five competitors? If so, your research is not specific enough yet. The quick tip on why consulting and why this firm has more, and networking for consulting shows how to have the conversations that give you those specifics.

Common mistakes

  • Leading with exit opportunities. They may matter to you, but they are not why you want this job.
  • Pretending prestige and pay never cross your mind. You do not need to mention them, but implausible purity sounds rehearsed. Focus on the work.
  • Reciting the firm's values back. The interviewer wrote them. Tell them something they do not know: your experience.
  • Running long. Two reasons, well evidenced, beat five asserted ones. Stay around 60 seconds.

Try it now

1. Improve this line: "I'm passionate about solving complex business problems."

Show the answer

Replace the claim with evidence: "Last year I worked out why our renewal rate had dropped from 85% to 70%, and finding the cause, a pricing change nobody had linked to it, was the best part of my year." Then connect it: "I want that kind of problem to be the whole job."

2. Apply the stress test to: "I'm drawn to your collaborative culture and your commitment to client impact."

Show the answer

It fails: almost every firm says this about itself. Swap in something you learned first-hand, such as what a consultant told you about how teams are staffed, or a practice area that matches your background.

3. Write your answer in five or six sentences: one signpost, two reasons each backed by a real moment, and a close.

Show the answer

Check it against the three tests: is there a specific moment, does it show you know what the job involves, and does it explain why now? If any is missing, the answer is not finished. Then say it aloud until it sounds natural rather than recited.

Where to practise next

This answer usually follows "Tell me about yourself", so make sure the two connect. If you are not sure which kind of consulting you want, the types of consulting will help you be specific.
